title: Gentle exercises in bed (for those who find it hard to get up or are recovering)
intro: If it's hard to get up or you're recovering, you can still move a little in bed to keep your blood flowing and maintain strength. These exercises are slow, short, and can be done lying down.
muscles: Calves, thighs, glutes, stomach (core muscles) and shoulders. The aim is to keep your joints moving, blood flowing, and basic strength, not to burn fat in specific areas.
steps: Ankle pumps: lying down, slowly move your toes up and down, 10 times.
Heel slides: bend one knee by sliding your heel towards your bottom, then straighten it again.
Glute squeeze: tighten your glute muscles for 3-5 seconds, then release.
Knee press: place a rolled towel under your knee, press your knee down for 3-5 seconds.
Arm raises: slowly lift both arms over your head as far as is comfortable, then lower them.
Breathe in deeply through your nose, breathe out slowly through your mouth, 5 times.
mistakes: Holding your breath while moving. Breathe normally the whole time.
Forcing the movement until it hurts. Only move within a comfortable range.
Moving too fast. These exercises should be slow and controlled.
easier: Do just one or two movements, 5 times each. Ankle pumps and deep breathing alone are already a good start.
harder: Once stronger, try a small bridge: bend your knees, lift your bottom slightly off the bed, hold 2-3 seconds, lower. Or sit at the edge of the bed and straighten one leg forward, alternating sides.
dose: 5-10 reps per movement, 1 round. Do 1-3 times a day, every day if your body feels okay. One session is about 5-10 minutes.
safety: Stop if there is sharp pain, dizziness, shortness of breath or chest pain. If you recently had surgery, are injured, or are under treatment, get clearance from your doctor or physio first and follow their instructions.

faq.q: Do these bed exercises really help?
faq.a: Yes. When you lie down for a long time, muscles weaken quickly and joints get stiff. These small movements help maintain strength and blood flow until you're ready to get up and walk.

faq.q: Can I do these after giving birth or after an operation?
faq.a: Every case is different. After giving birth, especially by C-section, or after other operations, ask your doctor or physio first about when and which movements suit you.

faq.q: When can I start standing exercises?
faq.a: When you can sit at the edge of the bed and stand steadily without feeling dizzy, try standing while holding onto a chair or wall. Start by walking around the room. If you are still recovering, follow your doctor's or physio's advice.
